A radiative-transfer solver needs, in every layer and at every spectral point, three things: how strongly the layer
attenuates light, what fraction of the attenuation is scattering, and in which directions the scattered light goes.
pyharp computes them in *opacity sources*: modules that turn the state of a layer (concentrations, pressure,
temperature, droplet size) into an extinction coefficient, a single-scattering albedo and phase-function moments.
A band lists its sources in the radiation YAML; this chapter describes how a source is selected and what it must
return, and then the sources of the chapter one by one: Rayleigh scattering by gas molecules, liquid-water droplets
by Lorenz-Mie theory, and a pre-mixed correlated-k table. A fourth source the code contains, the Helios table, is
refused whenever a band asks for it. How a band sums its sources into one solver input is the subject of the
assembly chapter, not of this one.

### Summary

A band does not compute optical properties itself. Its YAML entry lists the names of opacity sources, each name is
an entry of the `opacities:` block, and the entry's `type` chooses the C++ module that computes that source. This
section states the contract every source keeps: what it is given, the shape and units of what it returns, and how
the band sizes the buffer that receives it. The sections after this one describe the sources of the chapter.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** One module per listed source; output layout @eq-ch06-sources-out, buffer width @eq-ch06-sources-nprop.

**Data.** Molar concentrations in; $k_a$ [$\mathrm{m^{-1}}$], $\omega_a$, $\chi_{a,l}$ per spectral point and layer out.

**Placement.** Built when the band is built; evaluated at every band forward call.

**Activation.** `opacities: <name>: {type: ...}`, listed in the band's `opacities`; `type` is required.

**Guarantee / limits.** Unknown types and unknown species are refused before any computation.

**Evidence.** See the Tests layer below.
:::

Local symbols: $a$, index of an opacity source of a band; $s$, index of a species; $c_s$, molar concentration of
species $s$ [$\mathrm{mol\,m^{-3}}$]; $k_a$, extinction coefficient of source $a$ [$\mathrm{m^{-1}}$]; $\omega_a$,
its single-scattering albedo [-]; $\chi_{a,l}$, its phase-function moment of order $l$ [-], $\chi_{a,0} = 1$;
$n_{\mathrm{mom},a}$, the number of moments it returns [count]; $n_{\mathrm{prop}}$, the last dimension of the band's
`prop` buffer [count]; $\nu$, wavenumber [$\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$]; $\lambda$, wavelength [$\mu\mathrm{m}$].

### Derivation

**The spectral coordinate.** A source receives the spectral grid in two forms, the wavenumber $\nu$ and the
wavelength $\lambda$, related by

$$
\lambda = \frac{10^{4}}{\nu} .
$$ {#eq-ch06-sources-lambda}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch06-sources-lambda check_ch06_rayleigh.py [C4] -->

The factor $10^4$ converts centimetres to micrometres. @eq-ch06-sources-lambda is applied in
`RadiationBandImpl::forward` ({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}),
which writes both keys into the keyword arguments of every source from the band's wavenumber grid, overwriting
values the caller passed. A source called directly from Python accepts either key.

**What a source returns.** Every source returns one tensor of shape $(n_{\mathrm{wave}}, n_{\mathrm{col}},
n_{\mathrm{lyr}}, n_{\mathrm{prop},a})$. Along the last dimension it holds, at each spectral point, column and layer,

$$
\bigl(k_a,\ \omega_a,\ \chi_{a,1},\ \dots,\ \chi_{a,n_{\mathrm{mom},a}}\bigr),
\qquad n_{\mathrm{prop},a} = 2 + n_{\mathrm{mom},a} ,
$$ {#eq-ch06-sources-out}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch06-sources-out check_ch06_sources.py [C2] -->

for a source that scatters, and only $k_a$ ($n_{\mathrm{prop},a} = 1$) for a source that only absorbs. The moment
$\chi_{a,0} = 1$ is never stored. The moments follow the convention of DISORT: the phase function is
$P(\cos\Theta) = \sum_l (2l+1)\,\chi_l\, P_l(\cos\Theta)$, with $\Theta$ the scattering angle and $P_l$ the Legendre
polynomial of order $l$.

**The width of the band's buffer.** The band adds the sources into one buffer `prop`, whose last dimension must hold
the widest source:

$$
n_{\mathrm{prop}} = \max\Bigl(1,\ \max_a n_{\mathrm{prop},a}\Bigr) .
$$ {#eq-ch06-sources-nprop}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch06-sources-nprop check_ch06_sources.py [C1] -->

@eq-ch06-sources-nprop is computed in `RadiationBandImpl::reset`
({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::reset repo=pyharp >}}), which also raises
$n_{\mathrm{prop}}$ to 3 when the band's solver is Toon. Nothing in this contract is approximated; each source's
own approximations are stated in its section. The check is `check_ch06_sources.py` (Tests layer).

### Numerical method

There is no numerical method in the selection itself: it is a lookup by string, done once when the band is built.
@fig-ch06-sources-contract shows the tensor a source returns.

## Rayleigh scattering by gas molecules (`type: rayleigh`) {#sec-ch06-rayleigh}

### Summary

Molecules scatter light much shorter than their size with a cross section that grows as the inverse fourth power
of the wavelength: this is why a clear sky is blue and why a deep gas atmosphere reflects ultraviolet light. The
Rayleigh source (`type: rayleigh`) adds this scattering to a band. It computes the cross section of molecular
hydrogen from a published fit, scales it by a fixed factor for each other gas, multiplies by the molar
concentrations, and returns a purely scattering layer with the Rayleigh phase function.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** Gas scattering $k$ by @eq-ch06-rayleigh-k; phase function @eq-ch06-rayleigh-phase.

**Data.** Molar concentrations of the listed species in; $k$ [$\mathrm{m^{-1}}$], $\omega = 1$, $\chi_2 = 1/10$ out.

**Placement.** One source of a band; evaluated at every band forward call.

**Activation.** `type: rayleigh`, `species: [...]` (at least one), `nmom` $\ge 2$; off unless listed.

**Guarantee / limits.** Exact port of the fit; no depolarisation correction; eight species.

**Evidence.** See the Tests layer below.
:::

Local symbols: $\sigma_{\mathrm{H_2}}$, the cross section of $\mathrm{H_2}$ [$\mathrm{cm^2}$ per molecule] in
@eq-ch06-rayleigh-sigma and [$\mathrm{m^2\,mol^{-1}}$] after @eq-ch06-rayleigh-k; $\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}$, the
wavelength in units of $10^{-10}$ m [-]; $f_s$, the scale factor of species $s$ [-]; $N_{\mathrm{A}}$,
Avogadro's constant [$\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$]; $c_s$, $k$, $\omega$, $\chi_l$, $\Theta$, $\nu$ as in
@sec-ch06-sources.

### Derivation

**The cross section of molecular hydrogen.** The source uses the fit of Dalgarno and Williams (1962) for the
Rayleigh cross section of $\mathrm{H_2}$, a sum of three inverse even powers of the wavelength in units of $10^{-10}$ m (the
angstrom), $\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} = 10^{8}/\nu$:

$$
\sigma_{\mathrm{H_2}} = \frac{8.14\times10^{-13}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}^{4}}
  + \frac{1.28\times10^{-6}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}^{6}} + \frac{1.61}{\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}^{8}} .
$$ {#eq-ch06-rayleigh-sigma}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch06-rayleigh-sigma check_ch06_rayleigh.py [C1] -->

The first term is the $\lambda^{-4}$ law of a small polarisable particle; the other two correct for the variation of
the molecule's polarisability with frequency, and they matter in the ultraviolet (@fig-ch06-rayleigh-sigma).

**From a cross section to an extinction coefficient.** A cross section per molecule [$\mathrm{cm^2}$] becomes a
cross section per mole [$\mathrm{m^2\,mol^{-1}}$] by multiplying by $N_{\mathrm{A}}$ molecules per mole and by
$10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2\,cm^{-2}}$. The extinction coefficient of a layer is the sum over the configured species of
the molar concentration times the molar cross section, and the source takes every species' cross section to be
that of $\mathrm{H_2}$ times a constant factor $f_s$:

$$
k = \sigma_{\mathrm{H_2}}\, N_{\mathrm{A}}\, 10^{-4} \sum_s f_s\, c_s .
$$ {#eq-ch06-rayleigh-k}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch06-rayleigh-k check_ch06_rayleigh.py [C1] -->

@eq-ch06-rayleigh-sigma and @eq-ch06-rayleigh-k are computed in `RayleighImpl::forward`
({{< code src/opacity/rayleigh.cpp RayleighImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}), with $N_{\mathrm{A}}$ the constant
`Avogadro` ({{< code src/constants.h Avogadro repo=pyharp >}}). The factors $f_s$ are those of
@tbl-ch06-rayleigh-scales, which the code attributes to Pierrehumbert (2010).

| species | $f_s$ | species | $f_s$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{H_2}$ | 1 | $\mathrm{N_2}$ | 4.6035 |
| $\mathrm{He}$ | 0.0641 | $\mathrm{O_2}$ | 3.8634 |
| $\mathrm{H_2O}$ | 3.3690 | $\mathrm{CO_2}$ | 10.5611 |
| $\mathrm{CH_4}$ | 10.1509 | $\mathrm{NH_3}$ | 7.3427 |

: Scale factors of the Rayleigh source, from `species_scale` in rayleigh.cpp; names are matched without regard to case. {#tbl-ch06-rayleigh-scales}

**The phase function and its moments.** Light scattered by a small isotropic particle has the phase function
$P(\cos\Theta) = \tfrac34\,(1 + \cos^2\Theta)$, normalised so that its mean over the sphere is 1. Its moments
$\chi_l = \tfrac12\int_{-1}^{1} P(\mu)\,P_l(\mu)\,\mathrm{d}\mu$ follow from writing $\mu^2$ in Legendre
polynomials, $\mu^2 = \tfrac13 + \tfrac23 P_2(\mu)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(\mu) &= \tfrac34 + \tfrac34\left(\tfrac13 + \tfrac23 P_2(\mu)\right) \\
       &= 1 + \tfrac12 P_2(\mu) \\
       &= \sum_l (2l+1)\,\chi_l\,P_l(\mu) ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch06-rayleigh-phase}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch06-rayleigh-phase check_ch06_rayleigh.py [C3] -->

so $\chi_0 = 1$, $(2\cdot2+1)\,\chi_2 = \tfrac12$, that is $\chi_2 = \tfrac{1}{10}$, and every other moment is
zero. Rayleigh scattering by a gas absorbs nothing, so $\omega = 1$. Both are set
in `RayleighImpl::forward` ({{< code src/opacity/rayleigh.cpp RayleighImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}): the albedo
column is filled with 1 and the moment column $l = 2$ with 0.1; all other moments stay zero.

Nothing is truncated in the port: @eq-ch06-rayleigh-sigma and @eq-ch06-rayleigh-k are evaluated as written and
@eq-ch06-rayleigh-phase is exact. The approximations are those of the model: the fit itself, constant factors
$f_s$ for the other gases, and no depolarisation (Limits). The check is `check_ch06_rayleigh.py` (Tests layer).

### Numerical method

The source evaluates @eq-ch06-rayleigh-sigma once per spectral point and adds one product per configured species,
in every column and layer. There is no grid, no iteration and no stopping criterion; the cost is one tensor
operation per species. @fig-ch06-rayleigh-sigma shows the cross section the code returns and how much of it comes
from the two correction terms.

### Summary

Cloud droplets are spheres of water whose size is comparable to the wavelength, so neither the small-particle law
of @sec-ch06-rayleigh nor geometric optics describes them. Lorenz-Mie theory solves the scattering of a plane wave
by a homogeneous sphere exactly, as an infinite series of multipole terms. The liquid-water source
(`type: water-liquid-mie`) evaluates that series for droplets of one radius, takes the refractive index of water
from a table, and turns the droplet efficiencies into the extinction coefficient, single-scattering albedo and
phase moments of a layer that holds a given amount of liquid water.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** $k$ by @eq-ch06-mie-k from the Mie efficiencies @eq-ch06-mie-q; moments by @eq-ch06-mie-hg.

**Data.** Liquid-water concentration [$\mathrm{mol\,m^{-3}}$] and droplet radius `re` [$\mu\mathrm{m}$] in.

**Placement.** One source of a band; evaluated at every band forward call.

**Activation.** `type: water-liquid-mie`, one species, `nmom` $\ge 1$; `re` required at forward; off unless listed.

**Guarantee / limits.** Matches an independent reference to $10^{-9}$ for $x \ge 0.18$; see Limits below.

**Evidence.** See the Tests layer below.
:::

parameter [-]; $m = n_{\mathrm{r}} - \mathrm{i}\,n_{\mathrm{i}}$, complex refractive index of water [-], with
$n_{\mathrm{r}} > 0$ and the absorption index $n_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 0$; $a_j$, $b_j$, the Mie coefficients of order

@eq-ch06-mie-small [-]; $\rho_{\mathrm{w}}$, density of liquid water [$\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$]; $M$, molar mass of

### Derivation

**Size parameter.** A droplet of radius $r$ in light of wavelength $\lambda$ (both in $\mu\mathrm{m}$) has the size
parameter

$$
x = \frac{2\pi r}{\lambda} ,
$$ {#eq-ch06-mie-x}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch06-mie-x check_ch06_mie.py [C3] -->

computed in `mie_size_parameter`
({{< code src/opacity/water_liquid_mie_impl.h mie_size_parameter repo=pyharp >}}). The efficiencies depend only on
$x$ and $m$.

**Efficiencies from the Mie coefficients.** For a homogeneous sphere, the field outside is a sum of multipoles of
order $j = 1, 2, \dots$ with the electric and magnetic coefficients $a_j$ and $b_j$ (Bohren and Huffman 1983,
eq. 4.53). The extinction and scattering efficiencies, the cross sections divided by the geometric cross section
$\pi r^2$, are (their eqs. 4.61 and 4.62; Wiscombe 1980, eqs. 1a and 1b)

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q_{\mathrm{ext}} &= \frac{2}{x^2} \sum_{j=1}^{N} (2j+1)\,\mathrm{Re}\,(a_j + b_j) \\
Q_{\mathrm{sca}} &= \frac{2}{x^2} \sum_{j=1}^{N} (2j+1)\,\bigl(|a_j|^2 + |b_j|^2\bigr) ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch06-mie-q}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch06-mie-q check_ch06_mie.py [C1] -->

@eq-ch06-mie-q is computed in `mie_efficiency_device`
({{< code src/opacity/water_liquid_mie_impl.h mie_efficiency_device repo=pyharp >}}). The asymmetry parameter, the
mean cosine of the scattering angle, is given by Bohren and Huffman's equation 4.74 and Wiscombe's equation 1c:

$$
g = \frac{4}{x^2 Q_{\mathrm{sca}}} \left[ \sum_{j=1}^{N-1} \frac{j(j+2)}{j+1}\,
      \mathrm{Re}\bigl(a_j a_{j+1}^{*} + b_j b_{j+1}^{*}\bigr)
    + \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{2j+1}{j(j+1)}\,\mathrm{Re}\bigl(a_j b_j^{*}\bigr) \right] ,
$$ {#eq-ch06-mie-g}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch06-mie-g check_ch06_mie.py [C1] -->

with $^{*}$ the complex conjugate. @eq-ch06-mie-g is computed in the same function
({{< code src/opacity/water_liquid_mie_impl.h mie_efficiency_device repo=pyharp >}}), which also enforces
$Q_{\mathrm{ext}} \ge Q_{\mathrm{sca}}$ by setting $Q_{\mathrm{ext}} \leftarrow Q_{\mathrm{sca}}$ when round-off
inverts them, and clamps $g$ to $[-0.999999, 0.999999]$.

**The coefficients.** With the Riccati-Bessel functions $\psi_j(x) = x\,j_j(x)$ and $\xi_j(x)$, built from the
spherical Bessel functions of the first and second kind, and $D_j$ the logarithmic derivative of $\psi_j$ at $mx$,
the coefficients are

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_j &= \frac{\left(D_j/m + j/x\right)\psi_j(x) - \psi_{j-1}(x)}{\left(D_j/m + j/x\right)\xi_j(x) - \xi_{j-1}(x)} \\
b_j &= \frac{\left(m D_j + j/x\right)\psi_j(x) - \psi_{j-1}(x)}{\left(m D_j + j/x\right)\xi_j(x) - \xi_{j-1}(x)} .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch06-mie-ab}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch06-mie-ab check_ch06_mie.py [C1] -->

This is Bohren and Huffman's eq. 4.88, which follows from their eq. 4.53 by writing the derivatives of $\psi_j$ at
$mx$ through $D_j$. The code advances $\psi_j$ and $\xi_j$ with the three-term recurrence
$\psi_{j+1} = (2j+1)\,\psi_j/x - \psi_{j-1}$ (the same for $\xi_j$) from $\psi_0 = \sin x$,
$\psi_1 = \sin x/x - \cos x$.

**The series is truncated.** The code keeps the orders $j \le N$ with Wiscombe's criterion,

$$
N = \left\lfloor x + 4.05\,x^{1/3} + 2 \right\rfloor ,
$$ {#eq-ch06-mie-nstop}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch06-mie-nstop check_ch06_mie.py [C1] -->

which Wiscombe (1980) gives for $8 < x < 4200$; the code applies it at every $x$. It is computed in `mie_nstop` ({{< code src/opacity/water_liquid_mie_impl.h mie_nstop repo=pyharp >}}).

**Small droplets.** For $x \ll 1$ only the electric dipole term survives. To leading order in $x$, with
$\alpha = (m^2 - 1)/(m^2 + 2)$, the coefficient is $a_1 = -\tfrac{2\mathrm{i}}{3}\,x^3\alpha^{*}$ in the
convention of Bohren and Huffman (sec. 5.1), whose refractive index is the complex conjugate of ours; $b_1$ and the
higher orders are $O(x^5)$. Since $\mathrm{Re}\,(-\mathrm{i}\,\alpha^{*}) = -\mathrm{Im}\,\alpha$, inserting $a_1$
into @eq-ch06-mie-q gives, to leading order,

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q_{\mathrm{sca}} &= \frac{2}{x^2}\cdot 3\,|a_1|^2 = \frac{8}{3}\,x^4\,|\alpha|^2 \\
Q_{\mathrm{abs}} &= \frac{2}{x^2}\cdot 3\,\mathrm{Re}\,a_1 = -4x\,\mathrm{Im}\,\alpha \\
Q_{\mathrm{ext}} &= Q_{\mathrm{sca}} + Q_{\mathrm{abs}} ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch06-mie-small}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch06-mie-small check_ch06_mie.py [C2] -->

with $g = 0$; $\mathrm{Im}\,\alpha \le 0$ when $n_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 0$, so $Q_{\mathrm{abs}} \ge 0$. The neglected
terms are smaller by a factor of order $x^2$. `mie_efficiency_device` uses @eq-ch06-mie-small for $x < 10^{-3}$
({{< code src/opacity/water_liquid_mie_impl.h mie_efficiency_device repo=pyharp >}}).

**From efficiencies to the optical properties of a layer.** One droplet has the extinction cross section
$Q_{\mathrm{ext}}\pi r^2$ and the mass $\tfrac43\pi r^3\rho_{\mathrm{w}}$, so its extinction per unit mass of water
is $3Q_{\mathrm{ext}}/(4\rho_{\mathrm{w}} r)$. A layer with $c$ moles of liquid water per cubic metre holds $cM$
kilograms of it, so

$$
k = c\,M\,\frac{3\,Q_{\mathrm{ext}}}{4\,\rho_{\mathrm{w}}\, r} ,
$$ {#eq-ch06-mie-k}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch06-mie-k check_ch06_mie.py [C3] -->

with $r$ in metres, $M$ the molar mass of the configured species and $\rho_{\mathrm{w}} = 997\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$
unless `water_density` is given. The albedo is $\omega = Q_{\mathrm{sca}}/Q_{\mathrm{ext}}$. Both are computed in
`water_liquid_mie_properties_from`
({{< code src/opacity/water_liquid_mie_impl.h water_liquid_mie_properties_from repo=pyharp >}}).

**Phase moments.** The source does not return the Mie phase function. It returns the moments of a
Henyey-Greenstein phase function with the Mie asymmetry parameter,

$$
\chi_l = g^{\,l}, \qquad l = 1, \dots, n_{\mathrm{mom}} ,
$$ {#eq-ch06-mie-hg}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch06-mie-hg check_ch06_mie.py [C4] -->

so the first moment is exact and the higher ones are those of the Henyey-Greenstein shape; this is done in
`MieWaterLiquidImpl::forward` with `henyey_greenstein`
({{< code src/opacity/water_liquid_mie.cpp MieWaterLiquidImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}).

**The refractive index of water.** Unless the caller overrides it, $m$ comes from the table of Segelstein (1981),
854 rows of $\lambda$, $n_{\mathrm{r}}$, $n_{\mathrm{i}}$ from 0.1 to 1000 $\mu\mathrm{m}$. Between the rows
$\lambda_0 \le \lambda \le \lambda_1$ it interpolates in $\ln\lambda$, linearly for $n_{\mathrm{r}}$ and for
$\ln n_{\mathrm{i}}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\phi &= \frac{\ln\lambda - \ln\lambda_0}{\ln\lambda_1 - \ln\lambda_0} \\
n_{\mathrm{r}} &= n_{\mathrm{r},0} + \phi\,(n_{\mathrm{r},1} - n_{\mathrm{r},0}) \\
\ln n_{\mathrm{i}} &= \ln n_{\mathrm{i},0} + \phi\,(\ln n_{\mathrm{i},1} - \ln n_{\mathrm{i},0}) ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch06-mie-nk}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch06-mie-nk check_ch06_mie.py [C5] -->

and linearly in $n_{\mathrm{i}}$ itself where either row has $n_{\mathrm{i}} = 0$. This is done in
`water_refractive_indices` ({{< code src/opacity/water_liquid_mie.cpp water_refractive_indices repo=pyharp >}}).

What is exact and what is not: @eq-ch06-mie-q to @eq-ch06-mie-ab are exact for a homogeneous sphere; the series is
truncated by @eq-ch06-mie-nstop; @eq-ch06-mie-small neglects terms of relative order $x^2$; @eq-ch06-mie-hg keeps
only the first moment of the Mie phase function; the droplets all have the radius $r$ (no size distribution). The
check is `check_ch06_mie.py` (Tests layer).

### Numerical method

`MieWaterLiquidImpl::forward` computes the efficiencies once for every pair of spectral point and distinct droplet
radius in the call, not once per cell, because they depend on nothing else, and then spreads them to the cells and
applies @eq-ch06-mie-k. For each pair, `mie_efficiency_device` runs these steps.

1. If $x < 10^{-3}$, return @eq-ch06-mie-small.
2. Choose the direction of the recurrence for $D_j$. Following Wiscombe, it runs downward when $n_{\mathrm{r}} < 1$,
   $n_{\mathrm{r}} > 10$, $n_{\mathrm{i}} > 10$, or
   $x\,n_{\mathrm{i}} \ge 3.9 - 10.8\,n_{\mathrm{r}} + 13.78\,n_{\mathrm{r}}^2$, and upward otherwise.
3. Downward: start at order $N + 1$ from Lentz's continued fraction, which stops when successive ratios change by
   less than $10^{-12}$ (`lentz_log_derivative_device`,
   {{< code src/opacity/water_liquid_mie_impl.h lentz_log_derivative_device repo=pyharp >}}), and apply
   $D_{j-1} = j/(mx) - 1/(D_j + j/(mx))$. Upward: start from the closed form of $D_1$ and apply
   $D_j = 1/(j/(mx) - D_{j-1}) - j/(mx)$.
4. Evaluate @eq-ch06-mie-ab with the recurrences of $\psi_j$ and $\xi_j$, and sum @eq-ch06-mie-q and @eq-ch06-mie-g.

A failure (a non-positive $x$ or $n_{\mathrm{r}}$, a negative $n_{\mathrm{i}}$, too few scratch slots, or a
continued fraction that does not converge in $10^5$ steps) sets a status. A cell with a failed status gets
not-a-number, and the final check of `MieWaterLiquidImpl::forward` then refuses the result. In single precision the
recurrence runs in double for $x \le 0.5$. @fig-ch06-mie-accuracy shows the efficiencies and the error of the code
against an independent evaluation.

### Summary

Molecular absorption varies by orders of magnitude across a spectral band, too fast to resolve line by line in a
climate model. A correlated-k table replaces each band by a few quadrature points, each with an absorption cross
section tabulated against pressure and temperature. A *pre-mixed* table, as PICASO provides [@reading12;
@reading13], tabulates the cross section of the whole gas mixture at a given composition, so a single table covers
all absorbers at once. The source `type: picaso-ck` reads such a table from a NetCDF file and interpolates it to the
pressure and temperature of every layer.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** $k$ by @eq-ch06-picaso-k from the table interpolated by @eq-ch06-picaso-interp.

**Data.** Layer pressure `pres` [Pa], temperature `temp` [K] and concentrations in; $k$ [$\mathrm{m^{-1}}$] out.

**Placement.** One source of a band; evaluated at every band forward call.

**Activation.** `type: picaso-ck`, one `data` file; needs a NetCDF build; off unless listed.

**Guarantee / limits.** Exact for tables linear in the interpolation variables; clamps at the table edges.

**Evidence.** See the Tests layer below.
:::

Local symbols: $\kappa$, the tabulated cross section of the mixture [$\mathrm{cm^2\,mol^{-1}}$]; $q$, index of a
quadrature point of the table (a band and a g-point) [count]; $\nu_q$, its wavenumber [$\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$]; $p_i$,
the pressures of the table [Pa]; $T_{\mathrm{nom}}(p)$, the nominal temperature at pressure $p$ [K];
$\Delta T_j$, the tabulated temperature offsets [K]; $p$, $T$, the pressure and temperature of a layer;
$c_s$, $k$, $\nu$ as in @sec-ch06-sources.

### Derivation

**Where a layer sits in the table.** The table is not tabulated on temperature itself but on the offset from a
nominal temperature that depends on pressure, so that the few offsets cover the temperatures an atmosphere actually
has at each pressure. A layer at $(p, T)$ is placed at $\ln p$ and at the offset

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ln T_{\mathrm{nom}}(p) &= \mathcal{L}_p\bigl[\ln T_{\mathrm{nom}}(p_i)\bigr](\ln p) \\
\Delta T &= T - T_{\mathrm{nom}}(p) ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch06-picaso-tnom}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch06-picaso-tnom check_ch06_picaso.py [C1] -->

where $\mathcal{L}_p[\cdot](\ln p)$ is the piecewise-linear interpolation in $\ln p$ between the table pressures,
defined below. @eq-ch06-picaso-tnom is computed in `PicasoCKImpl::forward`
({{< code src/opacity/picaso_ck.cpp PicasoCKImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}).

**Interpolation.** For one axis with points $x_1 < x_2$ around the query $x$ and values $v_1$, $v_2$, the rule is

$$
\mathcal{L}[v](x) = \frac{(x - x_1)\,v_2 + (x_2 - x)\,v_1}{x_2 - x_1} ,
$$

and a query outside the axis takes the value at the nearest end. The source applies this rule axis after axis to
$\ln\kappa$, over the wavenumber of the quadrature points, $\ln p$ and $\Delta T$, and exponentiates the result:

$$
\kappa(\nu, p, T) = \exp\Bigl(\mathcal{L}_{\nu}\,\mathcal{L}_{p}\,\mathcal{L}_{\Delta T}\bigl[\ln\kappa(\nu_q, p_i,
\Delta T_j)\bigr]\bigl(\nu, \ln p, \Delta T\bigr)\Bigr) .
$$ {#eq-ch06-picaso-interp}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch06-picaso-interp check_ch06_picaso.py [C2] -->

@eq-ch06-picaso-interp is computed by `interpn` ({{< code src/math/interpn.h interpn repo=pyharp >}}), called from
`PicasoCKImpl::forward`. Interpolating $\ln\kappa$ linearly is interpolating $\kappa$ geometrically: halfway between
two points it returns their geometric mean.

**Extinction.** The table holds the cross section per mole of the whole mixture, so the extinction of a layer is the
cross section times the total molar concentration, with $10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2\,cm^{-2}}$:

$$
k = 10^{-4}\,\kappa(\nu, p, T) \sum_s c_s .
$$ {#eq-ch06-picaso-k}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch06-picaso-k check_ch06_picaso.py [C1] -->

@eq-ch06-picaso-k is computed in `PicasoCKImpl::forward`
({{< code src/opacity/picaso_ck.cpp PicasoCKImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}); the source returns $k$ alone
($n_{\mathrm{prop}} = 1$ in @eq-ch06-sources-out). The sum runs over every species column of the concentration
tensor.

@eq-ch06-picaso-k is exact. @eq-ch06-picaso-interp is exact where $\ln\kappa$ is linear in each of
$\nu$, $\ln p$ and $\Delta T$ between table points, and otherwise has an error of second order in the table
spacing of each axis. The check is `check_ch06_picaso.py` (Tests layer).

### Numerical method

When the band is built, `PicasoCKImpl::reset` reads the NetCDF variables of @tbl-ch06-picaso-vars, permutes `kappa`
into the order (band, g-point, pressure, temperature offset) whatever its order in the file, flattens band and
g-point into one axis of quadrature points, and stores $\ln\kappa$ with $\kappa$ floored at $10^{-300}$. At each
forward call the source evaluates @eq-ch06-picaso-tnom for every layer and @eq-ch06-picaso-interp at every spectral
point of the band, every column and every layer, in one call of `interpn`. @fig-ch06-picaso-table shows the
pressure and temperature axes.

| NetCDF variable | dimensions | unit as used |
|---|---|---|
| `quadrature_wavenumber`, `quadrature_weight` | (band, gpoint) | $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$; - |
| `wavenumber_lower`, `wavenumber_upper` | (band) | $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ |
| `pressure` | (pressure) | Pa |
| `temperature_offset` | (temperature_offset) | K |
| `nominal_temperature` | (pressure) | K |
| `kappa` | the four above, any order | $\mathrm{cm^2\,mol^{-1}}$ |

The check writes the tables it needs in the layout of @tbl-ch06-picaso-vars, so no PICASO data file is involved, and
reads the source through a band. Its `prop` buffer holds $k\,\Delta z$ (@sec-ch06-sources). On a table whose
$\ln\kappa$ is linear in $\nu$, $\ln p$ and $\Delta T$, stored with its four dimensions in reverse order, the band
returns @eq-ch06-picaso-k to below $10^{-14}$ relative at four quadrature points, two columns and three layers. On
a random table it matches a trilinear interpolation of $\ln\kappa$ written independently, to below $10^{-13}$.
Pressures of $10^2$ and $10^7$ Pa and temperatures of 100 and 900 K return the values at the table's edges, and
two splits of the same total concentration give bitwise equal $k$. A second data file and a file without `kappa`
are refused. A spectral point halfway between two quadrature points of different bands returns the geometric mean
of their $k$.[^ch06-pk-run] All of this runs on the CPU in double precision.

### Limits

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
- **The band's spectral grid must be the table's quadrature points.** The band always passes its own wavenumbers;
  a band wavenumber between two quadrature points gets a geometric mean of their cross sections, a value that
  belongs to neither ([C6]). The band's weights must equal the table's `quadrature_weight`; the source reads them
  but the band does not use them.[^ch06-pk-run]
- **Silent clamping.** A layer outside the table's pressures or temperature offsets gets the edge value, with no
  warning; `warn_out_of_bounds` is not read by this source.
- **Every species counts.** @eq-ch06-picaso-k sums all columns of the concentration tensor, so a condensate species
  in the state adds to the gas that absorbs.
- **NetCDF.** A pyharp build without NetCDF refuses the source when the band is built.
- **No test in pyharp.** The source is covered by this chapter's check only; with real PICASO tables it is not
  tested here.
:::

pyharp contains a module that reads a correlated-k table from a text file, named after the HELIOS code
[@reading17]: `HeliosImpl`,
and `RadiationBandImpl::reset` builds it for `type: helios`
({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::reset repo=pyharp >}}). No band can use it. The
constructor checks the type with `options->type().compare(0, 3, "helios") == 0`
({{< code src/opacity/helios.cpp HeliosImpl::HeliosImpl repo=pyharp >}}). That compares the first three characters
of the type, `hel`, with the six-character string `helios`; the two are never equal, so the check fails for every
non-empty type. The type `helios` is therefore refused with "Mismatch opacity type: helios", and any other spelling
never reaches the module, because `RadiationBandImpl::reset` refuses it first as an unknown type. Check
`check_ch06_sources.py` [C4] shows both: `helios` gives the mismatch message; `helios-ck`, `hel` and `Helios` give
"Unknown opacity type".[^ch06-hel-run]

Python has no class for the module (`pyharp.opacity` does not export it), so it cannot be built with an empty type
either. Read past the type check, the code would fail again: `HeliosImpl::reset` assigns the g-point weights
element by element to the member `weights`, which it never allocates
({{< code src/opacity/helios.cpp HeliosImpl::reset repo=pyharp >}}), and `HeliosImpl::forward` multiplies the table
by the concentration of species 0 rather than the configured species, under a comment that the units are still to
be checked ({{< code src/opacity/helios.cpp HeliosImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}). These two are read from the code
and not run. The test file `tests/test_helios_ck_read.cpp` belongs to an older code base (it includes headers that
pyharp does not have) and is not listed in `tests/CMakeLists.txt`, so ctest does not build it.

A reader who wants a correlated-k table in pyharp at the pin has the pre-mixed table of @sec-ch06-picaso. A reader
of HELIOS tables finds no working reader in pyharp at the pin.
